intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that Loeys-Dietz syndrome-5 (LDS5), also known as Rienhoff syndrome, is caused by heterozygous mutation in the gene encoding transforming growth factor-beta-3 (TGFB3; 190230) on chromosome 14q24.

checks.claim: Loeys-Dietz syndrome-5 (LDS5) is also known as Rienhoff syndrome.
checks.explanation: The paper never uses the names 'Loeys-Dietz syndrome-5' or 'Rienhoff syndrome'. It describes a new syndrome that it calls clinically distinct from LDS.

checks.claim: Loeys-Dietz syndrome-5 is caused by heterozygous mutation in the TGFB3 gene, which encodes transforming growth factor-beta-3.
checks.evidence_quote: We detected a novel heterozygous mutation in TGFB3, c.898C>G, predicting the missense substitution p.Arg300Gly. Sanger sequencing confirmed the mutation and its segregation with the phenotype.
checks.explanation: Heterozygous TGFB3 mutation segregating with a MFS/LDS-overlap disorder (Rienhoff syndrome).

checks.claim: The TGFB3 gene is located on chromosome 14q24.
checks.explanation: Only the abstract was available. It covers N-cadherin and left-right asymmetry in the chicken embryo. It never mentions TGFB3 or chromosome 14q24.

paragraphs.text: Loeys-Dietz syndrome-5 is an autosomal dominant connective tissue disorder. Its features overlap with those of Marfan syndrome and other forms of Loeys-Dietz syndrome. They include skeletal overgrowth or other skeletal features, joint laxity or contractures, craniofacial features such as hypertelorism and cleft palate or bifid uvula, and in some patients aortic or other arterial aneurysm and dissection. Like the other forms of Loeys-Dietz syndrome, it is caused by a defect in the TGF-beta signaling pathway; in this form, the mutated gene encodes the ligand TGFB3.

checks.claim: Loeys-Dietz syndrome-5 is an autosomal dominant connective tissue disorder.
checks.evidence_quote: The clinical overlap with these autosomal dominant syndromes and the unaffected status of the parents suggested a de novo mutation acting as a dominant trait in a gene affecting TGF-β signaling.
checks.explanation: The paper only suggests dominant action of a de novo mutation in one patient. It does not establish autosomal dominant inheritance or describe the disorder as a connective tissue disorder.

checks.claim: The features of Loeys-Dietz syndrome-5 overlap with those of Marfan syndrome and other forms of Loeys-Dietz syndrome.
checks.evidence_quote: We describe a syndrome presenting at birth with distal arthrogryposis, hypotonia, bifid uvula, a failure of normal post-natal muscle development without evidence of vascular disease; some features overlap with MFS and LDS.
checks.explanation: The paper states that the features overlap with Marfan syndrome and Loeys-Dietz syndrome.

checks.claim: Features of Loeys-Dietz syndrome-5 include skeletal overgrowth or other skeletal features.
checks.evidence_quote: Other systemic features overlap clinically with Loeys-Dietz, Shprintzen-Goldberg, and Marfan syndromes, including cleft palate, bifid uvula, skeletal overgrowth, cervical spine instability and clubfoot deformity.
checks.explanation: Skeletal overgrowth and other skeletal features reported.

checks.claim: Features of Loeys-Dietz syndrome-5 include joint laxity or contractures.
checks.evidence_quote: Also noted was bilateral pes planus, mild pectus excavatum, hyperextensibility of multiple large joints, and mild retrognathia.
checks.explanation: The patient had both joint hyperextensibility and digit contractures.

checks.claim: Features of Loeys-Dietz syndrome-5 include craniofacial features such as hypertelorism and cleft palate or bifid uvula.
checks.evidence_quote: She was hyperteloric and had a bifid uvula, the two non-vascular findings that define LDS
checks.explanation: The patient had hypertelorism and a bifid uvula; the claim's 'or' wording covers this.

checks.claim: Some patients with Loeys-Dietz syndrome-5 have aortic or other arterial aneurysm and dissection.
checks.evidence_quote: we clearly demonstrate that TGFB3 LOF mutations associate with aortic and other arterial aneurysms/dissections and mitral valve disease, and recognize an extremely variable cardiovascular phenotype
checks.explanation: Aortic and other arterial aneurysm/dissection in some patients; others lacked cardiovascular involvement.

checks.claim: Like other forms of Loeys-Dietz syndrome, Loeys-Dietz syndrome-5 is caused by a defect in the TGF-beta signaling pathway.
checks.evidence_quote: Several lines of evidence indicate the mutation is hypomorphic, suggesting that decreased TGFB signaling from a loss of TGFB3 activity is likely responsible for the clinical phenotype.
checks.explanation: The paper attributes the phenotype to a defect in TGF-beta signaling.

checks.claim: In Loeys-Dietz syndrome-5, the mutated gene encodes the TGF-beta ligand TGFB3.
checks.evidence_quote: The mature TGFB3 ligand is a homodimer of the C-terminal 112 amino acids of the TGFB3 mRNA translation product
checks.explanation: The mutated gene is TGFB3, which encodes a TGF-beta ligand.

paragraphs.text: The alternative name Rienhoff syndrome comes from Rienhoff et al. (2013), who first described the association of a TGFB3 mutation with this phenotype.

checks.claim: Rienhoff et al. (2013) first described the association of a TGFB3 mutation with the Loeys-Dietz syndrome-5 phenotype, giving rise to the alternative name Rienhoff syndrome.
checks.evidence_quote: This is the first example of a mutation in the coding portion of TGFB3 implicated in a clinical syndrome
checks.explanation: The paper claims priority for linking TGFB3 to a syndrome, but it says nothing about the name 'Rienhoff syndrome' or LDS5.

paragraphs.text: Rienhoff et al. (2013) described a girl whose syndrome combined low muscle mass, growth retardation, and distal arthrogryposis with clinical features overlapping those of Marfan syndrome and Loeys-Dietz syndrome. These features included hypertelorism, a cleft or bifid uvula/palatal abnormality, and skeletal findings.

checks.claim: Rienhoff et al. (2013) described a girl with a syndrome that included low muscle mass.
checks.evidence_quote: Her motor examination revealed decreased bulk in all appendicular and axial muscles, strength 1/5, low tone, and diminished reflexes throughout.
checks.explanation: The patient is female and had low muscle mass.

checks.claim: The girl described by Rienhoff et al. (2013) had growth retardation.
checks.evidence_quote: Among the inconsistencies with these diagnoses were significant growth retardation, the absence of cardiovascular findings, and the distinct muscle histopathology.
checks.explanation: The paper reports significant growth retardation.

checks.claim: The girl described by Rienhoff et al. (2013) had distal arthrogryposis.
checks.evidence_quote: Distal arthrogryposis indicative of reduced fetal movement suggested an inborn error of development
checks.explanation: The paper reports distal arthrogryposis.

checks.claim: The girl described by Rienhoff et al. (2013) had clinical features overlapping those of Marfan syndrome and Loeys-Dietz syndrome.
checks.evidence_quote: some features overlap with MFS and LDS
checks.explanation: The paper states the overlap with Marfan and Loeys-Dietz syndromes.

checks.claim: The girl described by Rienhoff et al. (2013) had hypertelorism.
checks.evidence_quote: Eyes appeared prominent and hypertelorism was present with an outer canthal distance of 7.8 cm and an inner canthal distance of 2.8 cm (>97th centile).
checks.explanation: The paper reports hypertelorism.

checks.claim: The girl described by Rienhoff et al. (2013) had a cleft or bifid uvula/palatal abnormality.
checks.evidence_quote: A bifid uvula with intact hard palate, normal arch, and normal voice quality were present.
checks.explanation: The patient had a bifid uvula; her hard palate was intact.

checks.claim: The girl described by Rienhoff et al. (2013) had skeletal findings.
checks.evidence_quote: the skeletal findings typical of MFS included arachnodactyly, pectus excavatum, pes planus, and hyperextensible large joints.
checks.explanation: The paper reports skeletal findings.

paragraphs.text: Bertoli-Avella et al. (2015) reported a series of patients from several families with heterozygous TGFB3 mutations. The patients had syndromic thoracic aortic aneurysm and dissection, and in some cases abdominal aortic or other arterial aneurysms. Other features included skeletal overgrowth, joint hypermobility or contractures, hypertelorism, bifid uvula or cleft palate, and other features of Loeys-Dietz syndrome. Vascular involvement varied within and between families.

checks.claim: Bertoli-Avella et al. (2015) reported a series of patients from several families with heterozygous TGFB3 mutations.
checks.evidence_quote: Here, we report on 43 patients from 11 families with syndromic presentations of aortic aneurysms caused by TGFB3 mutations.
checks.explanation: Mutations are described as heterozygous elsewhere in the text.

checks.claim: The patients with TGFB3 mutations reported by Bertoli-Avella et al. (2015) had syndromic thoracic aortic aneurysm and dissection.
checks.evidence_quote: We demonstrate that TGFB3 mutations are associated with significant cardiovascular involvement, including thoracic/abdominal aortic aneurysm and dissection, and mitral valve disease.
checks.explanation: Syndromic thoracic aortic aneurysm/dissection reported.

checks.claim: Some patients with TGFB3 mutations reported by Bertoli-Avella et al. (2015) had abdominal aortic or other arterial aneurysms.
checks.evidence_quote: Disease beyond the aorta, with iliac and subclavian artery aneurysms, was only identified in 2 patients (1-II:12 and 1-III:13).
checks.explanation: Abdominal aortic aneurysm/dissection and other arterial aneurysms reported.

checks.claim: Features in the patients with TGFB3 mutations reported by Bertoli-Avella et al. (2015) included skeletal overgrowth.
checks.evidence_quote: Other systemic features overlap clinically with Loeys-Dietz, Shprintzen-Goldberg, and Marfan syndromes, including cleft palate, bifid uvula, skeletal overgrowth, cervical spine instability and clubfoot deformity.
checks.explanation: Skeletal overgrowth stated.

checks.claim: Features in the patients with TGFB3 mutations reported by Bertoli-Avella et al. (2015) included joint hypermobility or contractures.
checks.evidence_quote: Other recurrent features include dolichocephaly, high-arched palate, retrognathia (with surgery in case 3-III:1), tall stature, joint hypermobility, arachnodactyly, pectus deformity, and inguinal hernia
checks.explanation: Joint hypermobility reported; contractures not mentioned.

checks.claim: Features in the patients with TGFB3 mutations reported by Bertoli-Avella et al. (2015) included hypertelorism.
checks.evidence_quote: Typical LDS findings such as hypertelorism, bifid uvula and cleft palate, cervical spine instability, and club foot deformity are commonly observed
checks.explanation: Hypertelorism reported (14 patients).

checks.claim: Features in the patients with TGFB3 mutations reported by Bertoli-Avella et al. (2015) included bifid uvula or cleft palate.
checks.evidence_quote: Typical LDS findings such as hypertelorism, bifid uvula and cleft palate, cervical spine instability, and club foot deformity are commonly observed
checks.explanation: Bifid uvula and cleft palate reported.

checks.claim: The patients with TGFB3 mutations reported by Bertoli-Avella et al. (2015) had other features of Loeys-Dietz syndrome.
checks.evidence_quote: The clinical phenotypes in the 10 additional families demonstrate significant overlap with Loeys-Dietz syndrome (Online Tables 3 to 6).
checks.explanation: Other LDS features (cervical spine instability, clubfoot, etc.) reported.

checks.claim: Vascular involvement in the patients with TGFB3 mutations reported by Bertoli-Avella et al. (2015) varied within and between families.
checks.evidence_quote: We observed a striking intrafamilial and interfamilial clinical variability with typical LDS features in some, but complete absence in others.
checks.explanation: Intra- and interfamilial variability is stated for clinical (LDS) features generally; vascular variability is described as extremely variable but not specifically within vs between families.

paragraphs.text: Transmission in the families reported by Bertoli-Avella et al. (2015) was consistent with autosomal dominant inheritance. The mutation in the patient described by Rienhoff et al. (2013) arose de novo.

checks.claim: Transmission of the disorder in the TGFB3 families reported by Bertoli-Avella et al. (2015) was consistent with autosomal dominant inheritance.
checks.evidence_quote: We studied a large Dutch family (family 1) with clinical features overlapping with MFS and LDS consistent with an autosomal dominant inheritance pattern.
checks.explanation: Autosomal dominant inheritance stated (explicitly for family 1).

checks.claim: The TGFB3 mutation in the patient described by Rienhoff et al. (2013) arose de novo.
checks.evidence_quote: Validation by Sanger sequencing confirmed that this mutation was de novo in the proband.
checks.explanation: The paper confirms the mutation arose de novo.

paragraphs.text: Rienhoff et al. (2013) found a de novo heterozygous missense mutation in the TGFB3 gene in a girl with the syndrome.

checks.claim: Rienhoff et al. (2013) found a heterozygous missense mutation in the TGFB3 gene in a girl with Loeys-Dietz syndrome-5.
checks.evidence_quote: The proband was heterozygous for two de novo mutations.
checks.explanation: The paper reports a heterozygous TGFB3 missense mutation, c.1226G>A (p.C409Y), in the girl. The paper does not use the label LDS5.

checks.claim: The TGFB3 missense mutation found by Rienhoff et al. (2013) in a girl with Loeys-Dietz syndrome-5 was de novo.
checks.evidence_quote: A second de novo mutation was found in TGFB3 (c.1226G>A; pC409Y). Validation by Sanger sequencing confirmed that this mutation was de novo in the proband.
checks.explanation: The paper confirms the TGFB3 mutation was de novo.

paragraphs.text: Bertoli-Avella et al. (2015) found heterozygous mutations in the TGFB3 gene in patients from multiple families with syndromic aortic aneurysm and dissection. The mutations segregated with the disorder in the families. As in other forms of Loeys-Dietz syndrome, aortic tissue from patients showed evidence of paradoxically increased TGF-beta signaling, even though the mutations were predicted to cause loss of function.

checks.claim: Bertoli-Avella et al. (2015) found heterozygous TGFB3 mutations in patients from multiple families with syndromic aortic aneurysm and dissection.
checks.evidence_quote: This revealed additional heterozygous TGFB3 mutations in 10 other probands (7 from Sanger sequencing and 3 from the exome sequencing cohort)
checks.explanation: Heterozygous mutations in 11 families with syndromic aortic aneurysm.

checks.claim: The TGFB3 mutations found by Bertoli-Avella et al. (2015) segregated with the disorder in the families.
checks.evidence_quote: This TGFB3 mutation (c.754+2T>C) segregated with the clinical phenotype and was also present in 1 young individual (1-IV:1, 17 years old) without documented cardiovascular features
checks.explanation: Segregation is explicitly reported only for family 1; family 6 mutation was de novo; segregation in other families not explicitly described.

checks.claim: The TGFB3 mutations found by Bertoli-Avella et al. (2015) were predicted to cause loss of function.
checks.evidence_quote: Similarly, molecular analyses and predictions based on the TGFB3 dimer model confirm that most TGFB3 mutations reported here cause LOF.
checks.explanation: Loss of function predicted/hypothesized for the mutations.

checks.claim: Aortic tissue from patients with TGFB3 mutations studied by Bertoli-Avella et al. (2015) showed evidence of paradoxically increased TGF-beta signaling, as in other forms of Loeys-Dietz syndrome.
checks.evidence_quote: Very similar to what has been detected in TGFB2-deficient aortic walls of humans and mice (8), we observed evidence of paradoxically enhanced TGF-β signaling in the aortic wall of a TGFB3 mutant patient, as shown by increased pSMAD2
checks.explanation: Paradoxical increase shown, consistent with other LDS forms, but signaling analysis was done in aortic tissue from a single patient (3-III:1), not multiple patients.
